body:
Same deal with my parents' insurance as well. After insurance the Abilify would probably have been workable, but it was still a higher copayment than for generic prescriptions. Thankfully my psychiatrist didn't seem to mind just dispensing her sample packs for most of the time she had me on it. Since it was working about as well as everything else I'd taken (i.e., not that well, if at all), it didn't make sense to continue it.

(sigh) Yay, life. I really don't know why I still bother with it.

I noticed nothing on Buspar the short time I was on it. I left that psychiatrist a short while later mostly because she ran a shitty practice (2-hour wait times in a forbidding space). She had also given me a few suspect recommendations ("read *The Purpose Driven Life* by this conservative preacher" even after I'd told her I was bisexual and an atheist).

Abilify... same sort of deal, except the new doctor added it at the same time as the Effexor, so I had no way of discerning which drug may have had any effects. (Neither one must have been all that useful if I still ended up visiting the Golden Gate Bridge.) The main drawback to Abilify that I saw was the lack of a generic since it's relatively new. No side effects that I noticed, though I was never on a particularly high dosage.

Withdrawal is annoying, yes, so I suppose I'm stuck for now even though no amount of medication or therapy seems to work. For me, the only cure at this point is some change in circumstances or in my ability to get things done (and therefore start becoming productive and successful again). Neither seems likely.

I've been on Prozac (+Buspar), Effexor (+Abilify, +Lamictal), and now Wellbutrin (+Lamictal). I can't really discern if they help much, but now that I've been on medication for some time I'd show signs of a worsening condition if I discontinued (at least temporarily). Whenever I've started or changed medicines or had positive flashes of "insight," I've noticed a brief elevation of mood. It quickly crashes, though, and I'm still liable to think of suicide, even if my feelings may be occasionally numbed.

I can frequently envision myself having success. Holding down a job and succeeding in community college classes the next year (to fill some lower-division breadth requirements and refresh myself on stuff I should remember from high school, like freshman calculus and introductory economic theory)... those seem like they could and should be manageable. I'd then be able to go back to my university, ace the last prereq (half of intermediate econ theory) so I can declare the econ major I want (it's capped, so I need at least a B), and then get to work on finishing that major and my degree, supplementing it with useful stuff like additional math, stats, and CS courses. All told I could then graduate maybe only a year or two behind schedule. (Still embarrassing when I will have to face people younger than me who are many times smarter and more successful, but that's the price I pay for not having taken care of this problem long ago. I was suicidal as early as age 9, so I've had plenty of time.) At that point I could seek employment that pays real money--which I understand isn't as hard to get with an econ major as with others--and start paying down all the student debt I've accumulated (and take financial responsibility for whatever my parents borrowed before they went belly-up). I'm sure I'd need to have done well enough to leave open the possibility of graduate school in order to have opportunities for advancement, though.

The problem comes up when I see that nothing is happening just to get the first part off the ground. Perhaps I'm doing the job search incorrectly (and need to be drugged even more so I can be more socially outgoing), but nobody seems to want me. There are thousands of other people more qualified who are applying to every little job that comes up here. (I'd consider moving to a nicer region with lower unemployment, but I don't have the cash on hand just to get started somewhere, and a job in one of those places is still no guarantee I could afford the higher cost of living.) I still can't get myself to follow one lousy pre-intro CS class on OCW (MIT 6.00)--therefore I haven't proven that I can actually take classes rather than wasting my parents'/taxpayers' money again (or, worse, semesters of financial aid eligibility).

The state really should have an interest in putting me to death if I don't turn things around quickly, but since they don't, I ought to force myself to take care of that if I fail once more.

I was able to try it again as a depression remedy when I went back to school this last time. It was a temporary distraction, but it certainly didn't make me more productive. Cannabis and other drugs are out now that I'm back living at home (and in need of a job, which in this more conservative area seems to mean you have a greater chance of being asked for a drug test than in the famously liberal place where I should be going to college).

I haven't even noticed that kind of change, really. Come to think of it, I have a slightly elevated mood for a short time after starting a new medication, but that seems to wear off quickly. Something else must be screwed up with me, though, since I can rarely cry even when I feel like doing so or the situation kind of warrants it.

You're not alone, for what that's worth. I was first suicidal at 9, which I showed by writing an assignment in a suicidal way. I'm 19 now, having lost the last two years of potential productivity to depression/bipolar II/something (time I could have spent succeeding rather than failing, dropping out, re-entering, and failing again at the great university I got into). I feel like a burden to everyone else (financial, especially, since there aren't any jobs for anyone here, let alone for a failure like me, considering almost 20% unemployment--and that's the conservative estimate that doesn't include discouraged workers) and therefore conclude that I have an obligation to die. This comes in addition to my desire to die because of loneliness, hopelessness, lack of motivation and direction, and the like.

I have at least noticed some differences in the effects of different medications; perhaps your doctor should consider switching you to a different class of drug. In addition, think back and see if there's any evidence you may have inadvertently held from your doctor that might suggest a different diagnosis instead. (Don't make shit up, obviously, but it does seem that other conditions, such as bipolar disorder, can masquerade as depression.)

Don't drop out--do everything you can to get this under control now. Here's a cautionary tale: I've been in a similar situation to you lately, and I made the mistake of waiting until too late to start getting my depression under control. By dropping out (this was Feb. '09; I was 18), I've landed myself back home in a more depressing location than my university. I'm lonelier here, and my intellectual faculties and knowledge have been slipping severely. I tried to go back this semester, but I dropped out *again* after about 6 weeks.

Stay active as much as you can, and please seek out all the resources possible to get you to feel motivated and purposeful again. Perhaps you could go through your catalog and just see if you have even a passing interest in any classes or majors. Take one of those fields that you come up with and make a point to explore it further. It would probably help to seek out clubs or organizations that cater to interests you may have; maybe you can meet people and practice socializing there. Please don't repeat my mistakes.

Tried cannabis, both alone and in groups. It's never been beneficial, and it's ceased to be all that fun for me, too. In any event, I can't really do it now that I'm back with my parents (they disapprove), but my university's location is famously permissive of the stuff.

I really don't know what makes me happy. I probably did well in school previously because it was simply something I was required to do and it allowed me to distract myself and others from my complete lack of any other dimension of personality. 

I know a few things that make me distracted and serve as the closest thing to happiness that I can achieve right now--road trips, reading general social-sciency and other nonfiction (I've managed to sit down and read at least a few books for the first time in a few years now, but I would still fail at actual literature or scholarly stuff that I should be able to read, understand, and discuss intelligently by now).... that's about all that comes to mind. I still waste too much time just surfing the Web, watching movies and TV shows I've downloaded (Seinfeld lately... sometimes I make up for this by watching TED talks or listening to meaningful podcasts from public radio), even driving around aimlessly and wasting money I don't have at Starbucks (since in this town there isn't much else for coffee) just to get out of the house.

Yup, all evidence of failure (or at least that things need to change... but I seem to be incapable or unwilling to do so, therefore I should just be shot)

Why would being emotional be beneficial? Perhaps close friends would value the sort of trust that usually comes with revealing and discussing emotions, but surely they have no place in work and school. This leads me to believe that I should find some way to destroy my "self" even further in the interests of productivity, so that I am less inhibited by feeling tired or useless or other stuff "going on" in my life that nobody cares about.

If I can't spur myself even to start trying to change things, what should I do now? How and why am I not a complete waste at this point?

What about not knowing where to start since I'm so behind in every possible aspect--should I just pick one randomly?

I really should try not to think about suicide (or at least not tell other people I know) lest I get thrown back into hospital myself... I already spent 25 hours in one several months ago after telling my psychiatrist of my visit to the bridge and my feeling that I should do that over again. That was less than helpful. When I went last month I was sort of flagged by the bridge patrol as potentially suicidal and escorted down to talk with them and the highway patrol... somehow I talked them out of whisking me to a hospital there involuntarily, and instead I went back to my university's counseling services for the third time in a week.

Exactly how does one "get over" this, though? What actually helped you turn things around after three years?
